glaux: Take your time. Let the colours guide your eye.
prompt: Arrange these stars from coolest surface to hottest.
hint: Blue stars are the hottest. Start with the coolest.
rightLine: The colours now run from cooler to hotter.
missedLine: Start with red, then orange, then blue. Follow how the heat changes.
explanation: For these star colours, surface heat increases from red through orange to blue.

glaux: Follow how quickly each star uses its fuel.
prompt: Two stars are in their steady stage. Which one usually lives shorter?

options.text: The heavier star.
The lighter star.
Both live the same time.

hint: Compare how quickly the fuel is used.
rightLine: Faster fuel use means a shorter life.
missedLine: The heavier star uses fuel faster. Follow that clue.
explanation: Heavier stars use fuel faster. The heaviest shine for only millions of years; the Sun for about ten billion.

prompt: Arrange our address from our planet to the widest view.
glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.

explanation: Earth belongs to our solar system, which belongs to the Milky Way, one galaxy in the universe.

prompt: A planet orbits another star in the Milky Way. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: It belongs to our solar system because it shares our galaxy.
It belongs to another planetary system in our galaxy; it could still be far from Earth.
It must be outside the Milky Way because it has another star.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: A galaxy contains many stars. A planet around another star belongs to a different planetary system, and sharing a galaxy does not establish closeness.

prompt: A rounded model has a 10 cm Sun, a 1 mm Earth and an 11 m gap. Double the whole model. What changes?

options.text: The Sun becomes 20 cm, Earth stays 1 mm, and the gap stays 11 m.
The Sun becomes 20 cm, Earth becomes 2 mm, and the gap stays 11 m.
The Sun becomes 20 cm, Earth becomes 2 mm, and the gap becomes 22 m.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: Doubling the whole model doubles every length: the objects’ widths and the gap between them.

prompt: A model has a 10 cm Sun, a 1 cm Earth and an 11 m gap. Compare it with our rounded model. What needs correcting?

options.text: Earth is drawn too large. The Sun’s width and the approximate gap match our model.
Only the gap is incorrect; Earth should stay 1 cm wide.
Nothing needs correcting because the Sun is bigger than Earth.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: Our Earth is about 1 mm wide, not 1 cm. Being smaller than the Sun is not enough: the relative sizes must also match.

prompt: An illustration shows large planets close together. What must you check before measuring a gap from it?

options.text: Whether the picture is attractive enough to be trusted.
Whether its caption says distances share one consistent scale; sizes may use another scale.
Only whether the planets appear in the correct order.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: A picture can show the correct order while shortening gaps or enlarging planets. Its stated scale determines what we can measure.

prompt: You widen the atlas view until Earth disappears. What happened?

options.text: Earth’s physical width became smaller.
Earth stopped belonging to the solar system.
The view’s scale changed. Earth still exists at its original physical size.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: Zooming changes the view, not the physical object. An enlarged marker can show an object too small to draw at that scale.

prompt: Someone places the nearest other star just beyond model Neptune, a little over 320 m away. Why is this misleading?

options.text: At the same scale, that star is roughly 3,000 km away. The gap has been greatly shortened.
It is misleading only because the star is drawn in another colour.
It is accurate because the next star comes after the last planet.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: Being the next star does not mean being just beyond the planets. The space between stars is enormous on this same model scale.

prompt: A traveller says: “I have left the solar system, so I have left the Milky Way.” Which correction explains the relationship?

options.text: Correct: the solar system and the Milky Way are two names for the same system.
Leaving the solar system can still leave the traveller inside the Milky Way, which contains our whole solar system.
Leaving the solar system means leaving the universe, but not the Milky Way.

glaux: Take your time. Look for the relationship.
hint: Return to the explanation and compare the relationships.
missedLine: Let us look at the explanation together.
explanation: Our solar system occupies a tiny part of the Milky Way. Crossing the boundary of the smaller system does not mean leaving the larger one.
